clue.text: Diana merits a whole new look

indicators.note: giving the words a whole new look means rearranging their letters into another order

explanation.surface: Someone decides that the goddess deserves a complete makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a whole new look' reads as the makeover, but only 'whole new look' signals the rearrangement: 'a' is part of the fodder, so MERITS plus A is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Diana is the Roman huntress goddess, matched by her Greek counterpart.

clue.text: His hero was bound to be released by Shelley

definitions.text: His hero was bound to be released by Shelley

parts.words: His hero was bound to be released by Shelley
parts.note: the hero is Prometheus: the Greek tragedian wrote Prometheus Bound, and Shelley answered it with Prometheus Unbound

explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Athenian dramatist is credited with Prometheus Bound, whose captive Titan Shelley's verse drama later set free.

clue.text: Oh! Sophonisba! Sophonisba! Oh!" (-)

parts.note: a famously bathetic line from the 1730 tragedy Sophonisba, by the Scottish poet who also wrote The Seasons; it was parodied as 'Oh! Jamie ...'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is simply the notorious line itself; the solver must name the poet James who wrote it.
explanation.definitionFit: James Thomson, author of The Seasons, wrote the tragedy containing this much-mocked line.

clue.text: War novelist madly ran to arms

indicators.note: running madly suggests the letters go wildly out of order and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A soldier dashes frantically to pick up his weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Monsarrat wrote The Cruel Sea, a celebrated novel of naval warfare.

clue.text: Edward Ward took one to the bath

definitions.text: Edward Ward took one to the bath

parts.words: Edward Ward took one to the bath
parts.note: Ned Ward, the satirist of the London Spy, published A ___ to the Bath in 1700, a pamphlet on a visit to the spa town of Bath

explanation.definitionFit: Ned Ward's pamphlet title uses this word for a pace or short journey towards the spa.

clue.text: His contribution seen as novel in Germany

definitions.text: His contribution seen as novel in Germany

parts.words: His contribution seen as novel in Germany
parts.note: Jörg ___, a sixteenth-century Alsatian writer, is often regarded as the founder of the German prose novel, so his work was a novelty as well as novels

explanation.definitionFit: Jörg Wickram's Der Goldtfaden and other works are counted among the first German novels.

clue.text: Humorist seen to dilute company

parts.note: to dilute a drink is to water it
a house is a firm or company, as in a publishing house

explanation.surface: A comic writer is spotted watering down the firm's assets.
explanation.definitionFit: Keith Waterhouse, author of Billy Liar and newspaper columns, was a celebrated comic writer.

clue.text: Drink in honour of Godwin hero

indicators.note: the drink is placed in the honour, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: CB stands for Companion of the Bath, a British honour
ale is a drink, a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A toast is raised to celebrate the hero of a novel by Godwin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink in honour of' reads as a toast, but 'in' is a container signal; the honour is the Companion of the Bath, a British order of chivalry.
explanation.definitionFit: William Godwin's novel Caleb Williams is named after its narrator and protagonist.

clue.text: Concert pianist could be wealthy (and fifty per cent better)

parts.note: wealthy means rich

indicators.note: fifty per cent of a word is half of it; here the back half of the six-letter word better is taken

explanation.surface: A concert performer might be rich, and half as good again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fifty per cent better' sounds like an improvement, but it takes the second half of BETTER, giving TER.
explanation.definitionFit: Sviatoslav Richter was a renowned Soviet virtuoso of the keyboard.

clue.text: Illusions of early Mexicans?

definitions.meaning: in Hindu philosophy maya is the illusion of the material world; the clue uses the plural
the pre-Columbian civilisation of Yucatán and Central America

explanation.definitionFit: Maya is Sanskrit for illusion, and the same word names the ancient people of Central America.

clue.text: No attitude with which to approach the sonnet, Wordsworth thought

definitions.text: No attitude with which to approach the sonnet, Wordsworth thought

parts.words: No attitude with which to approach the sonnet, Wordsworth thought
parts.note: Wordsworth's sonnet opens '___ not the Sonnet; Critic, you have frowned', urging readers not to despise the form

explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth's sonnet begins by telling critics not to show contempt for the sonnet.

clue.text: Actuality of organizing Henley, etc

indicators.note: organizing the letters means arranging them into a new order

explanation.surface: The reality of running the Henley regatta and similar events.
explanation.walkthrough: HENLEY plus ETC is rearranged; Henley is a Thames town famous for its rowing regatta.
explanation.definitionFit: In Aristotle's philosophy entelechy is the realisation of potential, the condition of being actual rather than potential.

clue.text: The Confectioner's Talea, a confection of Flecker

definitions.text: The Confectioner's Talea, a confection of Flecker

parts.words: The Confectioner's Talea, a confection of Flecker
parts.note: James Elroy Flecker's verse play has the full title The Story of ___ of Baghdad, and its hero is a confectioner, so the play is a sweet-maker's tale

explanation.walkthrough: 'Talea' is the OCR running together 'Tale, a'. 'Confection' plays on the hero's trade: he is a confectioner, and the play is something Flecker concocted.
explanation.definitionFit: Flecker's play is named after its hero, a confectioner of Baghdad.

clue.text: Hilda Doolittle paid them to Freud and other high fliers

definitions.text: Hilda Doolittle paid them to Freud and other high fliers

parts.words: Hilda Doolittle paid them to Freud and other high fliers
parts.note: the poet H.D. wrote Tribute to Freud and the war poem Tribute to the Angels; angels are the 'high fliers'

explanation.definitionFit: H.D. paid homage in two books whose titles begin with this word, one to Freud and one to the angels.

clue.text: Dictionary researcher's biographer's school

definitions.meaning: Simon ___ wrote The Surgeon of Crowthorne, the life of W.C. Minor who supplied quotations to the Oxford English Dictionary
an ancient English public school in Hampshire, founded in 1382

explanation.definitionFit: Simon Winchester is the author who told Minor's story, and Winchester College is a famous school.

clue.text: Attractions booked by Clark Blaise

parts.note: Clark Blaise's 1979 novel is titled ___ Attractions, so the attractions in the book are moon-related

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective meaning of the moon begins the title of Blaise's novel about attractions.

clue.text: Ballantyne subject with considerable pulling power

definitions.text: Ballantyne subject with considerable pulling power

parts.words: Ballantyne subject with considerable pulling power
parts.note: R.M. Ballantyne wrote The ___, a story of railway life; the phrase is a nickname for a steam locomotive, which pulls trains

explanation.definitionFit: A steam locomotive was nicknamed this, and Ballantyne made it the subject of a railway tale.

clue.text: Her best-known creation made Believe it or Not, believe it or not

definitions.text: Her best-known creation made Believe it or Not, believe it or not

parts.words: Her best-known creation made Believe it or Not, believe it or not
parts.note: the novelist's best-known character is Tom Ripley, and Ripley's Believe It or Not! is the famous series of oddities, so the name links the two

explanation.walkthrough: The novelist's creation shares his surname with Robert Ripley, whose Believe It or Not! catalogued curiosities; the clue pretends her character made that series.
explanation.definitionFit: Patricia Highsmith created the con man Tom Ripley, namesake of the Believe It or Not! franchise.

clue.text: Style Anne adapted in Victorian novel

indicators.note: something adapted has been altered, so these letters are rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: Anne's way of writing was turned into a nineteenth-century book.
explanation.definitionFit: East Lynne is Mrs Henry Wood's sensational 1861 bestseller, a staple of Victorian melodrama.

clue.text: Fast success in 1951

parts.note: Howard Fast self-published his novel about the rebel gladiator in 1951 and it became a bestseller, later filmed by Kubrick

explanation.definitionFit: Howard Fast's 1951 novel of the Thracian gladiator's revolt was a major success.

clue.text: Some of what archbishop Lang evinced concerning Plantagenets

indicators.note: only some of the letters in these words are used, a run lifted from inside them

explanation.surface: Part of what Archbishop Lang showed related to the medieval royal house.
explanation.walkthrough: Cosmo Lang was Archbishop of Canterbury; the run sits across 'LANG EVINced'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plantagenet kings descended from the Counts of Anjou, so anything relating to that dynasty is called by this adjective.

clue.text: Roman jurist happy in Paris and America

parts.note: gai is the French word for happy or cheerful
US is short for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A Roman lawyer is cheerful in France and the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaius was a second-century Roman legal writer whose Institutes became a standard textbook of law.

clue.text: "And the silent isles — The Lady of Shallott" (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "And the silent isles — The Lady of Shallott" (Tennyson)

parts.words: "And the silent isles — The Lady of Shallott" (Tennyson)
parts.note: the line in Tennyson's poem reads 'And the silent isle ___ / The Lady of Shalott': the island shelters or encloses her as in a bower

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is an old form meaning to enclose as in a bower; the gap after 'isles' stands for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic verb means to shelter or enclose within leafy cover, as the island encloses the Lady.

clue.text: Portents seriously regarded by Romans intent on war (I urge USA to change position)

definitions.text: Portents seriously regarded by Romans intent on war

indicators.note: asking the letters to change position means moving them about into a new order

explanation.surface: An aside urges America to rethink its stance while recalling Roman omens before battle.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket reads as political advice to the USA, but 'to change position' rearranges I URGE USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Romans consulted augurs, priests who read omens from birds before battles and public business.

clue.text: Brontë character not seen as black-and-white

definitions.text: Brontë character not seen as black-and-white

parts.words: Brontë character not seen as black-and-white
parts.note: Anne Brontë's heroine is surnamed Grey, a shade that is neither black nor white

explanation.definitionFit: Anne Brontë's governess-heroine bears the surname Grey, between black and white.

clue.text: Once more ignited in extempore literature

indicators.note: the answer sits in these words, its letters running across the join between them

explanation.surface: An improvised piece of writing sets the fire going again.
explanation.definitionFit: Something set burning again after going out has been kindled a second time.

clue.text: James portrayed her as a lady

definitions.text: James portrayed her as a lady

parts.words: James portrayed her as a lady
parts.note: Henry James's novel The Portrait of a Lady centres on its heroine ___ Archer

explanation.definitionFit: Isabel Archer is the heroine of Henry James's The Portrait of a Lady.

clue.text: Wren's was ideal

parts.note: P.C. Wren wrote ___ Geste, and the phrase '___ ideal' means a perfect model

explanation.walkthrough: Wren is the novelist P.C. Wren, not the architect; his hero's name also completes the phrase meaning a perfect type.
explanation.definitionFit: P.C. Wren's hero is Beau Geste, and 'beau ideal' names the perfect example.

clue.text: A little fiction

parts.note: a short or slight piece of romantic prose fiction, the diminutive of a long one

explanation.definitionFit: The word adds a diminutive ending to a long prose story, so it means a short one.

clue.text: Irish victory for Shaw

parts.note: a victory is a win

explanation.surface: An Irish triumph for the playwright Shaw.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw suggests George Bernard, the Irish playwright, but the definition is the first name of the American novelist Irwin Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: The American author of The Young Lions was called Irwin Shaw.

clue.text: Legislator a Nestor, perhaps, capable of treason

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters could be arranged differently, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: A lawmaker as wise as old Nestor might still be a traitor.
explanation.walkthrough: A NESTOR is rearranged; 'capable of treason' adds a second anagram, since TREASON's letters also make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a senate is one who makes laws.

clue.text: "She did not deign even to notice the unhappy cavalier whom she had thus as it were — d" (Disraeli, Sybil)

definitions.text: "She did not deign even to notice the unhappy cavalier whom she had thus as it were — d" (Disraeli, Sybil)

parts.words: "She did not deign even to notice the unhappy cavalier whom she had thus as it were — d" (Disraeli, Sybil)
parts.note: the missing verb in Disraeli's sentence means to throw a rider from his mount, used figuratively of the snubbed cavalier

explanation.definitionFit: To throw a rider from his mount; Disraeli uses it figuratively for a lady's snub.
